weeks.title: Business context and AI opportunities
blocks: Businesses combine natural resources, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and knowledge to create value. Retailers offer availability and convenience. Economic systems organise resources differently; inflation, employment and growth influence business decisions. Supply, demand and competition affect prices [1].

Concept Check, section 1.1: how do revenue, costs and profit differ? When a shopper buys bread at Magnum, the money received is revenue. The shop pays for the bread, wages and rent. Profit is what remains after all costs. Higher sales alone do not establish higher profit.

Company A is Carrefour SA, an international retailer with franchised operations: 15,415 stores under its banners at 30 June 2026 [2]. Company B is Magnum Cash&Carry, serving households and businesses in Kazakhstan. Magnum reported over 200 stores on 1 July 2026 [3]. Carrefour provides documented practices to compare; Magnum provides the local setting. The question is whether assisted ordering or search could improve service at an acceptable cost.
Table 1 · Environment and AI opportunity map
Affordability, costs and employment affect demand.
BNS, 1 Sep. 2026: annual inflation 9.8%, Aug. 2026/Aug. 2025. BNS, 14 Aug. 2026: real GDP +4.1%, H1 2026/H1 2025, flash estimate. BNS, 13 Aug. 2026: unemployment 4.5%, Q2 2026. [4], [5], [6]
Forecast sales; category managers verify errors and approve orders. Retain manual ordering.
Kazakhstan Personal Data Law, 21 May 2013, No. 94-V, art. 5: lawfulness, confidentiality, security. Checked 11 Sep. 2026. [7]
Assist rule searches; legal staff verify obligations. Use approved or aggregate data.
Online shopping encourages better search and availability.
BNS, 25 May 2026: e-commerce was 14.3% of total retail trade in 2025, including marketplaces; not grocery-specific. [8]
Pilot catalogue search. Verify product facts; retain ordinary search and staff support.
SMALL competes in Kazakhstan grocery retail.
SMALL, Small Tech, undated; accessed 11 Sep. 2026: retail network and technology infrastructure. AI deployment unconfirmed. [9]
Compare public offers; staff check matching products and dates.
Market size does not establish preferences or trust.
BNS, 1 Sep. 2026: population 20,604,819 as of 1 Aug. 2026. [10]
Analyze aggregate demand; test language preferences. Keep human complaint handling.
Import prices may affect procurement, but do not prove delays.
BNS, Statistics of prices, accessed 11 Sep. 2026: import-price index 101.6%, Jun. 2026/Jun. 2025 (+1.6%). Publication date unconfirmed. [11]
Flag invoice changes; procurement verifies alerts and approves decisions.
Source: the dated publications cited in each row. Effects and proposed AI uses require local testing.

Source checks with Codex matched the periods and values in the map: inflation, real GDP, unemployment, e-commerce, population and import prices. The Carrefour count includes franchise markets; Magnum’s count is a company statement. The e-commerce figure includes marketplaces. The import index of 101.6% means a 1.6% increase; its access date is used because the publication day is unspecified. These checks and source locations are recorded in the Evidence Folder.

The inflation evidence makes affordability relevant, but store sales and shopper feedback are needed to identify which products people will buy. GPT-6 Astra in the ChatGPT app helped with requirements and wording. Codex helped find and check sources, analyse course materials, draft revisions and format the document.

Carrefour launched Hopla in France on 8 June 2023 [12]. Magnum could test whether Kazakh and Russian questions lead to available catalogue items, with staff help when search fails. Forecasting needs a separate comparison against current ordering, using errors and stockouts. Managers should retain order approval and complaints. Expansion depends on benefits covering costs, protected customer data and a usable manual process.
The Evidence Folder records the company scale statements, Kazakhstan indicators and Carrefour’s Hopla announcement, with dates, links and claim checks. Source numbers match the Evidence Folder.
This record develops Capstone section 1, Business context, and sets the questions for the comparison.

weeks.topic: Business environment and sustainability: economic systems, ethics, global markets and SDGs
weeks.title: Ethics and stakeholders
blocks: Ethics concerns right and wrong. Utilitarianism weighs overall consequences, while duties and rights protect people whose interests might otherwise be overlooked. Managers influence behaviour through their example, training and reporting arrangements [1].

CSR includes economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities. These operate together [13]. Concept Check, section 2.3: give an example of legal but irresponsible behaviour [1]. A lawful promotion could encourage customers to buy food they cannot use. Donations would not remove that problem.

Comparative advantage means specialising where opportunity cost is lower. Imports come from abroad; exports go abroad. Trade balance is exports minus imports. Currency depreciation, transport costs and trade barriers can make foreign purchases more expensive [1].
Company B is Magnum Cash&Carry; Company A is Carrefour. Magnum’s history records entry into Uzbekistan in 2021 [14]. This establishes regional experience, not export volumes.

The proposed use is catalogue search. Magnum Club’s policy lists purchase histories and location data [15], creating a tension between useful recommendations and privacy. My priorities are customers, who bear direct harm; regulators, who influence permitted processing; and employees, who correct mistakes. Suppliers need fair visibility. Owners need a viable trial, while communities bear waste consequences.
Table 2 · Stakeholder and AI ethics map
Check stock and labels; test both languages; retain staff help.
Hopla links budget questions to product search [12].
Train staff, log corrections and assign a service manager.
AI supports product descriptions; staff workload is unreported [12].
Check descriptions with suppliers and allow corrections.
Carrefour generated descriptions for its own brands [12].
Customer data may reach external providers.
Review data flows, restrict access and retain records.
Carrefour describes Azure privacy features, not an independent audit [12].
Source: Carrefour’s launch announcement [12]. The Magnum controls and transfer decisions are proposals.

Checks with Codex on 20 September 2026 matched the Uzbekistan entry year to Magnum’s history [14], data categories to policy section 4.3 [15], and Hopla’s launch to Carrefour’s release of 8 June 2023 [12]. The release gives no measured error rate or staff savings. I therefore removed implied proof of effective oversight. NIST supports named responsibilities and training [16]; it does not certify Magnum.

The evidence refines my initial view: faster service matters only if shoppers can rely on it. Codex helped analyse the textbook and slides, check sources, draft the stakeholder analysis and edit this record. The checks distinguish company announcements from measured performance.

PILOT catalogue search after privacy review. The digital team should test Kazakh and Russian questions against available products, comparing errors and staff correction time with ordinary search. A service manager should resolve complaints and pause the trial after harmful recommendations. DELAY purchase-history personalisation until its purpose and benefit are demonstrated.

Carrefour also proposes recipes using leftover ingredients [12]. Magnum could adapt this idea to products approaching expiry, with stock and safety checks. Store managers should compare discarded food per unit sold before and during the trial, linking it to SDG 12.3 [17]. This is a proposed measure, not a reported result.
Carroll [13], NIST [16] and UN Goal 12 [17] extend the Evidence Folder. Company sources are reused. Course material: Chapter 2 and 3 slides and BA Week 2 Practice 2, slides 7–16.
This record develops Capstone section 2, Environmental and stakeholder analysis, and supports Business Report section 2.

weeks.topic: Ownership, entrepreneurial mindset and business models
weeks.title: Ownership and business model
blocks: Ownership affects control, finance and risk. A sole proprietor has direct control but unlimited personal liability. Partners share resources and decisions; liability depends on the form. A corporation is a separate legal entity, with ownership held through shares. Entrepreneurs seek opportunities under uncertainty, while intrapreneurs develop ideas within an existing organisation [1].

Concept Check, section 5.1: what differentiates an entrepreneur from a small-business owner? Entrepreneurship emphasises innovation and growth; an owner may instead prioritise a stable operation. At Magnum, an employee proposing a forecasting trial would be acting as an intrapreneur.

Carrefour SA operates an international retail model that includes franchises [2]. Magnum identifies itself as an LLP [15]. Kazakhstan’s partnership law generally limits participants’ risk to their contributions, subject to exceptions, and makes their general meeting the highest governing body [18]. This legal form does not reveal Magnum’s beneficial owners or its internal approval limits.

Magnum creates value by making goods available to households and business customers [14]. Sales generate revenue; purchases, wages, premises and logistics consume it. Forecasting could reduce tied-up stock and waste, while catalogue search could make shopping easier. Both also add software and staff costs. Magnum Club already provides digital loyalty interaction [15], although the policy does not establish AI deployment.
Table 3 · AI Business Model Stress Test
Hopla and later shopping services link questions to products. [12], [19]
Recommendations may point to unavailable goods.
Test Kazakh and Russian questions against the local catalogue. Compare successful searches; keep staff help.
SAS describes AI for demand forecasts and ordering. [20]
Stock errors or promotions make forecasts unreliable.
Compare stockouts, waste and correction time with current ordering. Category managers approve orders.
Ethics charter covers conduct and reporting. [21]
Written commitments may not change purchasing.
Apply accountability through existing Magnum rules. [22] Track resolution and repeated complaints.
Extra data may add intrusion and cost without enough benefit.
Review purpose, access and customer choices. Demonstrate value beyond existing Magnum Club offers. [7], [15]
A proposed extension beyond the documented comparison.
Keep a named manager and manual ordering for this trial. This is the proposed Magnum boundary.
Source: company and vendor publications cited in the table. Verdicts and test conditions are proposed for Magnum.

Changed assumption: the trial finds that recorded stock differs from shelf stock during promotions. The forecasting verdict changes from PILOT to DELAY: category managers first reconcile stock and promotion records, then retest against current ordering. Search remains limited to items with checked availability. Expansion requires savings from fewer lost sales and less waste to exceed software, integration, training and correction costs. These are decision criteria, not measured Magnum results.

This test supports Capstone section 3 and Business Report section 3. It narrows the investment case: improve availability with accountable staff before using more customer data. Preparation and source checks were supported by Codex.

sheet.title: Activity 3 AI Business Model Stress Test
blocks: Magnum should test forecasting and adapt catalogue search, retaining staff approval. The table separates existing activities from proposed AI uses and expected benefits.
Magnum serves household shoppers and business buyers through retail and wholesale activities.
Help shoppers find available products through questions in Kazakh or Russian, reducing search effort.
Uncertainty: shoppers may prefer ordinary search. Language errors could suggest unsuitable products.
Carrefour, 8 Jun. 2023: Hopla connects questions about budgets, dietary needs and meals to product search.
ADAPT: use Magnum’s catalogue and both languages. Test successful searches and retain staff help.
Stores provide access to goods. Magnum Club adds bonuses, discounts and offers based on customer interests.
Offer relevant basket suggestions; using purchase histories could extend personalisation beyond the shopper’s current request.
Ambiguity: additional data may not improve relevance enough to justify privacy concerns.
Hopla responds to preferences supplied by shoppers. This supports useful suggestions without establishing a need for Magnum’s purchase histories.
DELAY additional personalisation: establish purpose, privacy controls and benefits beyond existing offers. Start with the shopper’s stated needs.
Retail and wholesale operations require replenishment. The sources do not establish Magnum’s forecasting method or stock-data quality.
Forecast demand by product and store; suggest quantities that category managers review before ordering.
Volatility: promotions or delivery changes can quickly alter demand and stock needs.
SAS, 14 Jan. 2019: Carrefour selected SAS Viya to improve forecasts and supplier ordering using store, warehouse and online data.
PILOT one category against current ordering. Compare stockouts and waste; retain manual approval because local accuracy is unproven.
Magnum has store and commercial teams and a loyalty application. These sources do not establish AI capabilities.
Draft catalogue descriptions and support purchasing documents, while staff verify product facts and decisions.
Complexity: product data, suppliers, staff skills and software must work together. Errors add correction work.
Carrefour, 8 Jun. 2023: AI enriches product descriptions and supports tender drafting and quote analysis for non-retail purchasing.
ADAPT assistance to local products and workflows. REJECT autonomous approval for this trial; managers remain accountable.
Retail and wholesale sales generate revenue. Profit depends on covering goods and operating costs; loyalty discounts affect margins.
Reduce lost sales and waste through better availability. Deduct software, integration, training and correction costs from expected benefits.
Ambiguity: higher sales may reflect promotions rather than AI, and may not mean higher profit.
SAS links Carrefour’s forecasting project to availability and reduced overstock. The announcement gives no measured return applicable to Magnum.
PILOT the business case. Finance and category managers should compare net benefits with current practice before expansion.
Sources: Carrefour, Magnum Cash&Carry and SAS. Proposed uses and verdicts are the analysis for Magnum.

Suppose a promotion reveals that recorded stock differs from shelf stock. Forecasting changes from PILOT to DELAY until category managers reconcile the records. Search must then show only checked availability, staff need time to correct data, and the financial test must include that work. Retest against current ordering before expansion. This is a stress scenario, not a reported Magnum incident.
Sources checked 30 September 2026. Company and vendor announcements establish the examples; Magnum’s results require local testing.
Carrefour. Carrefour integrates OpenAI technologies and launches a generative AI-powered shopping experience. 8 June 2023.
Magnum Cash&Carry. Magnum Club personal data privacy policy. undated. Sections 2.4 and 4.3.

weeks.topic: Management and leadership: planning, organising, leading and motivating
weeks.title: Management, responsibility and human–AI task allocation
blocks: Management connects planning, organising, leading and controlling. Setting a target is only the first step: managers must provide resources, explain responsibilities and respond when results fall short. Chapter 7 distinguishes authority from responsibility and explains how reporting relationships support coordination [1].

Concept Check, section 7.4: how does the chain of command clarify reporting relationships? For the proposed Magnum trial, staff would report stock discrepancies to the category manager. The manager could obtain IT support without passing the purchasing decision to the software. Participative leadership would let store employees challenge forecasts using what they see on the shelves [1].

Magnum’s retail and wholesale activities make replenishment a relevant process [14]. I propose a six-month forecasting trial in one store and product category, with the category manager accountable for ordering. Week 3 identified inaccurate promotion and stock records as a reason to delay the trial. Those records must therefore be checked first.
The matrix separates producing a recommendation from committing money. It describes proposed roles; public company material does not establish Magnum’s current allocation of these tasks.
Approve the final order and handle exceptional commitments.
The category manager checks stock, shelf life and budget, records the decision and remains accountable [1], [16], [22].
Interpret promotion effects and unusual demand.
AI highlights patterns; staff add local knowledge and challenge misleading suggestions. Store feedback informs the manager’s decision [1].
Produce demand forecasts and draft order quantities.
Carrefour’s forecasting example supports testing this use [20]. The manager checks inputs, unusual quantities and supplier limits before accepting or changing each order.
Check missing fields and timestamps; record versions and approvals.
These are fixed rules, not AI purchasing decisions. Failed checks block the draft and notify staff. Logs make errors traceable [16].

If records disagree or a forecast fails, staff stop the affected recommendation and alert the category manager. Unresolved supply problems go to the supply-chain lead; technical faults go to IT. Staff use a physical stock count and verified sales to prepare a manual order for the same manager’s approval. Training should include rejecting a poor forecast and practising this fallback.

The course text was checked for management functions, participative leadership and reporting relationships [1]. NIST supports explicit responsibilities and staff training [16]. The SAS announcement describes Carrefour’s forecasting work, but it does not establish Magnum’s performance or guarantee savings [20]. GPT-6.1 Sol helped find these sources, and draft the matrix.
The important distinction is authority: automating calculations does not mean delegating the right to place an order.

PILOT Carrefour’s forecasting approach after reconciling local data [20]. Adapt it to Magnum’s category, promotions and supplier lead times. Keep final approval with a named manager. Do not expand if staff cannot explain the forecasts, correct errors or operate the manual process.

The Evidence Folder links the textbook [1], Magnum’s company description [14], NIST [16] and the SAS announcement [20] to their specific claims. The proposed management roles are an application of these sources, not a published Magnum organisation chart.
This record supplies the human–AI operating model for Assignment 2 and the capstone.

sheet.title: Week 4 Human AI Task Allocation Matrix
blocks: Process: replenishment in one Magnum store and product category. Pilot the forecast and draft quantities; retain a named manager’s approval. The roles below are proposed for the trial.

Approve orders and budget exceptions
Owner: Category manager
Financial commitment and product acceptance need named accountability. Textbook §7.4; Magnum rules.
Check stock, shelf life and budget. Reject or amend before release.

Interpret promotions and supply constraints
Owner: Planner with store staff
Local knowledge complements forecasts. Participative leadership and employee voice support challenge.
Staff document changes and reasons. Manager reviews exceptions.

Forecast demand and draft order quantities
Owner: Model, reviewed by category manager
Forecasts can process sales patterns, but record errors can distort quantities. Carrefour offers a precedent, not local proof.
Compare with sales, count, promotions and supplier limits. No order release without approval.

Check required fields and data age; log approved orders
Owner: Fixed rules maintained by IT
Repeatable checks have explicit pass or fail criteria and a traceable record. This stage does not use AI judgment.
Missing or stale input blocks the affected recommendation and alerts staff.
Basis: OpenStax management and authority [1]; Magnum’s stated rules [22]; NIST oversight [16]; Carrefour’s forecasting example [20]. Numbers refer to the cumulative Evidence Folder.

The category manager owns the order decision. Store staff challenge forecasts and record the reason for changes. The supply-chain lead handles unresolved supply issues, while IT handles technical faults. These support roles do not remove the manager’s approval responsibility.

Stop affected AI recommendation. Staff use a physical count and verified sales to draft a manual order. The category manager approves it. The manager authorises restart only after the problem is corrected and checked. Use aggregate product/store data, restrict access and practise the manual routine before the trial [15], [16], [22].

weeks.topic: Business performance: production, operations and supply chain management
weeks.artifact: Current- and future-state process map with KPI, escalation and fallback
weeks.title: Replenishment, controls and performance
blocks: Operations management coordinates people, materials and information to deliver a useful service at an acceptable cost. Resource planning balances availability against the cost of holding stock. A process map shows where work passes between people and where a delay or error can affect the whole service [1].

Concept Check, section 10.4: how is technology used in resource planning? It can combine sales and stock data to support purchasing. The benefit depends on accurate inputs and workable decisions. Faster calculations alone will not fill an empty shelf, and a forecast should not become a purchase without review.

The process is replenishment of one product category in one Magnum store. Its retail activities and product acceptance rules establish the context [14], [22]. The current-state sequence below is an evidence-informed baseline to confirm with staff; it is not an observed account of Magnum’s internal procedures. The proposed bottleneck is reconciling stock and promotion information before deciding quantities.
Automated: validate sales and stock inputs; block failed checks.
Estimate demand and order quantity using the existing method.
AI Executes with Human Review: forecast demand and draft quantities.
An authorised manager approves the order.
Human + AI: staff interpret promotions and supplier constraints. Human Only: the category manager checks exceptions and approves or changes the order.
Send the order and receive goods.
Send only the approved order and receive goods.
Check shelf availability and costs. Automated logs preserve inputs, revisions and approvals for review.

If records disagree or a forecast fails, staff stop the affected recommendation and alert the category manager. Unresolved supply problems go to the supply-chain lead; technical faults go to IT. Staff prepare a manual order from verified sales and a physical stock count. The category manager approves it and authorises any restart after correction. No unapproved order is sent [16].

The following six-month pilot targets are proposals, not Magnum results. Establish a baseline before starting, use the same products and checking schedule, and compare results with the existing ordering method.
Available product checks ÷ all scheduled checks × 100. Target: at least 98%.
Sum of absolute forecast errors ÷ sum of actual units sold × 100. Target: a 10% relative reduction from baseline.
Proposed reductions of 10% each in expired/damaged stock value and staff cost per order. Include software, training and correction costs when assessing net benefit.

Lost sales during stockouts can conceal demand, so WAPE must be interpreted alongside shelf availability. The category manager should review exceptions daily and trends weekly, using store feedback to explain unusual results [1].

Carrefour’s documented forecasting initiative makes PILOT a defensible transfer decision [20]. Week 3’s stock-data problem remains a stop condition. Expand only if availability reaches the target, forecast error improves, net benefit remains positive and staff can use the fallback. This map provides the operations argument and on-screen evidence for Assignment 2.

sheet.title: Week 5 main artifact: current-state to future-state process map
blocks: Selected process: Replenishment of one product category in one Magnum store (the Week 4 process). Week 3 AI opportunity: AI demand forecasting with draft order quantities (Stock planning: PILOT).
Current state is a baseline to confirm with Magnum staff: public sources establish the retail and product-acceptance context, not the internal ordering workflow [14], [22].
Read sales and stock levels for the category from store records.
Human + System: store staff with the stock system
Check promotions and supplier limits such as delivery days.
Estimate demand and order quantity with the existing method.
Send the order; receive and accept goods.
Human + System: purchasing and receiving staff
Check shelves; record availability and expired or damaged stock.

Bottleneck, steps 2–3 — stock records and promotion information are reconciled by hand before quantities are set. During promotions recorded stock can differ from shelf stock (Week 3 stress test), so orders can be too large or too small, causing stockouts or waste. Working hypothesis to confirm with Magnum staff.

Current KPI: Shelf availability = checks with the product available ÷ all scheduled checks × 100. Supporting: forecast error (WAPE). Current value: not published by Magnum. Record a baseline before the pilot, using the same products and checking schedule.
Validate sales and stock inputs: missing fields, data age.
Failed or stale input blocks the recommendation and alerts staff.
Forecast demand and draft order quantities.
AI, reviewed by the category manager
Draft only; it cannot be sent. The existing method runs on the same inputs for comparison.
Adjust for promotions, delivery days and supplier limits.
Both: planner and store staff with AI flags
Each change and its reason is recorded.
Approve, change or reject the order.
Checks physical stock, sales, promotions, shelf life and budget. No release without approval.
Send the approved order; receive and accept goods.
Both: purchasing and receiving staff with the system
Only approved orders can be sent. Goods are accepted under Magnum rules [22].
Check shelves and costs; log inputs, revisions and approvals.
Both: store staff and automated log
Manager reviews exceptions daily and trends weekly.

Step 4. The category manager checks physical stock, sales, promotions, shelf life and budget before any AI-drafted order is released, and approves, changes or rejects it. Staff may challenge a forecast at Step 3 [1], [16].
AI → Category manager (data or forecast issue) → Supply-chain lead (unresolved supply issue). Technical fault → IT. Repeated failures pause the trial.

Stop the affected AI recommendation. Staff count physical stock and use verified sales to draft a manual order; the category manager approves it and the process rejoins at Step 5. Restart only after the manager confirms the fault is corrected [16].

Shelf availability. Current: to be measured (not public). Target: ≥ 98%. Also: WAPE 10% below baseline; waste value and staff cost per order 10% lower each; net benefit positive. Proposed pilot targets, not Magnum results.
Fewer empty shelves, less expired or damaged stock, less staff time per order and lower forecast error, tested against current ordering.
The category manager approves, changes or rejects every order, authorises restart after a failure and stays accountable; staff add local knowledge.
Augmented: forecasts and draft quantities (AI executes, human reviews) and promotion adjustments (human + AI). Fixed-rule automation, not AI: input checks and logs. Approval is not automated.

Risk: wrong stock or promotion records give confident but wrong quantities. Control: input checks, manager approval and WAPE read with shelf checks; if recorded and shelf stock differ, DELAY until reconciled (Week 3 stop condition).

Company B should PILOT AI demand forecasting with draft order quantities in one store and product category for six months, keeping the category manager’s approval for every order, because Carrefour’s forecasting initiative shows the practice is worth testing [20], while Magnum’s data quality, results and costs stay unproven until they are compared with current ordering.

weeks.topic: Markets and customers: marketing functions, selling strategies and the buying process
weeks.title: Customer value, pricing and promotion
blocks: Marketing starts from customer value: the benefits a customer receives compared with the price and effort of buying. A firm combines product, price, place and promotion to deliver that value to a chosen target market [1]. Pricing decides how much of that value the firm captures, and promotion informs, persuades and reminds; sales promotion adds a short-term reason to buy now [1].

Concept Check, section 11.9: what is the difference between penetration pricing and price skimming? Penetration sets a low price to win market share quickly; skimming starts high and lowers the price later. A mature grocery category leaves little room to skim, so value depends on clear, credible offers.

Concept Check, section 12.8: how does sales promotion differ from advertising? Advertising builds awareness over time through paid media; sales promotion offers a temporary incentive, such as a discount, coupon or bonus, to trigger an immediate purchase. Magnum’s weekly Пайда programme is a sales promotion.

Magnum’s target segment is budget-conscious households doing a weekly family shop. Annual inflation was 9.8% in August 2026 [4], and Magnum Club reports more than 2 million members [24]. Пайда listed 51 products for 15–21 October, discounted by 18–53% [23]. Of the six products reduced by 50% or more, four were household or personal-care items; staples in the list (eggs, bananas, chicken fillet) were reduced by only 18–22% [23].

The friction point lies between consideration and purchase. The Пайда page attracts attention, but its “up to 60%” promise was not met that week, and it offers no store link or Magnum Go button [23], [25]. The Week 6 artifact therefore compared two ways of writing the same weekly message from the same 51-product list.
Prices and dates match the catalogue
Met: checked against the saved list
Met: nearest store or Magnum Go
Met: facts from the list only

Limitations: the test covered one week and one message, the baseline’s authorship was assumed, and no customer response was measured. Two weaknesses in the AI draft were caught only by checking: it offered Magnum Go although Пайда price validity there was unconfirmed [25], and it picked a laundry gel rather than a food staple.

Prices and discounts were checked against the Пайда list saved on 17 October [23]; the maximum discount and the food and non-food split were recalculated from that file. Carrefour’s figures were checked in its press releases [12], [19], and carrefour.fr was opened on 17 October to confirm that Hopla is still live [29]. Claude (Anthropic) generated the AI-supported draft that was tested and helped draft this record and its figures.

ADAPT. Carrefour enriches more than 2,000 own-brand product sheets with generative AI [12], and its product pages carry this kind of marketing copy [30]. Magnum can adapt the practice for its weekly Пайда messages, but only with a fact-check gate, Kazakh-language review and no personal data in the tool. Shopping inside ChatGPT [19] is DELAY: it needs catalogue and checkout integration that this record has not assessed.

weeks.title: Information, AI workflow and governance
blocks: Data are raw facts; information is data organised so that someone can act on it. A management information system turns transaction data into reports and decision support; its value depends on accurate inputs, clear responsibilities and protection against unauthorised access, malware and human error [1].

Concept Check, section 13.1: how do data and information differ? A list of 51 products with prices is data; a verified message telling a family which deal saves the most, until when and where to buy is information. Data become valuable when they support a better decision.

Concept Check, section 13.5: why are privacy advocates alarmed by data warehouses and data mining? Combining records from many sources can reveal detailed profiles that customers never agreed to share, and a larger store of data makes a breach more harmful.

The decision continues Week 6: each week, which Пайда deal to feature and which message to send to which Magnum Club segment, using the pricing system, the Magnum Club CRM and app, Magnum Go, an approved AI tool and a dashboard. Internal system names are not public, so roles are assumed [23]–[25].

In the proposed workflow the AI tool receives only the public promo list and drafts three messages; segments are built inside the CRM using consent flags. A copywriter checks every price, date and claim, a native speaker checks the Kazakh text, and the brand manager approves. Personal data stay in Kazakhstan, where Law 94-V requires them to be stored [7].
Privacy (medium / high): member data in prompts or stored abroad [7], [24]
Only the public promo list goes to AI; segments built inside the CRM. Owner: person responsible for personal data
Monthly prompt-log audit: no personal data
Reliability (medium / medium): wrong price, date or claim
Automatic price check plus copywriter sign-off; no send on mismatch. Owner: brand manager
All messages pass the check before sending
Bias (medium / medium): deepest discounts favoured over staples; weaker Kazakh copy
At least one food staple each week; native review in both languages. Owner: CRM manager
Food and non-food mix; results by language
Accountability (low / high): no record of who approved an error; tool outage
Approval log names the approver; manual template fallback. Owner: head of marketing with IT security [16]
Complete approval log; quarterly fallback drill

Uncertain cases go to the brand manager, personal-data issues to the person responsible for personal data, and AI-labelling questions to legal. If the AI tool or the check fails, the copywriter uses an approved template with the same checks; if the CRM is down, no push is sent. This fallback is not hypothetical: on 17 October Carrefour’s Hopla assistant showed a loading error twice [29].

The legal points were read on adilet.zan.kz: Law 94-V, articles 7, 12 and 16 [7], and AI Law No. 230-VIII, articles 17, 18 and 21 [27]. The CNIL decision was read in EDPO’s unofficial English translation, which links to the CNIL original [26]. Claude (Anthropic) helped draft this record and the workflow diagram; the risk ratings are qualitative judgements. Open question: whether AI-drafted copy edited by people needs an AI label under article 21; legal should decide before a pilot.

ADOPT the controls, DELAY the personalisation. Carrefour’s Hopla uses purchase history but warns users not to enter personal data [29], and the CNIL fined Carrefour France €2.25 million partly for keeping the loyalty data of 28 million inactive customers for 5–10 years [26]. Magnum should first set retention limits, an AI-use notice and fast opt-out, adjusted to Kazakhstan’s storage rule and AI Law [7], [27], before any personalisation with purchase history.
The Evidence Folder links sources [7], [16], [23]–[27] and [29] to their claims and holds the Week 7 workflow diagram and the Hopla screenshot.

blocks: Magnum should concentrate on reliable product availability and affordable shopping, testing AI where it can help with these tasks. Magnum Cash&Carry is a Kazakhstan-based retailer that also serves business customers through wholesale operations [1]. Carrefour, Company A, provides a comparison because its public reporting covers an international retail business with franchised operations [2]. This report focuses on Magnum’s Kazakhstan business. Carrefour’s experience can suggest what to test, but cannot establish what Magnum will earn from it.

The economic issue carried forward from Weekly Record 1 is affordability. Kazakhstan’s annual inflation was 9.8% in August 2026, according to the Bureau of National Statistics release of 1 September [3]. This makes price and purchasing decisions important, although it does not tell us which products Magnum shoppers will choose. Store sales and customer feedback are needed before changing an assortment.

BNS also reported that e-commerce represented 14.3% of Kazakhstan’s retail trade in 2025 [4]. This includes marketplaces and is not a grocery-specific measure. It supports examining digital shopping, rather than assuming customers want an AI assistant. SMALL’s retail and technology presence provides a relevant local comparison [5]. Magnum therefore needs to judge any proposed improvement against ordinary shopping and ordering, including whether the extra cost is justified. A convenient search tool has limited value when the recommended item is unavailable.

Weekly Record 2 prioritises customers, regulators and employees for the proposed catalogue-search trial. Customers bear the direct consequences of unsuitable recommendations. Regulators influence permitted data processing, while employees must identify errors and handle complaints. Suppliers need accurate descriptions and fair visibility; owners need a viable business. Communities are affected by waste. Magnum’s corporate rules address customer safety, supplier selection and reporting concerns [6]. These commitments establish expectations, but do not show how consistently individual stores meet them.

The clearest ethical tension concerns loyalty data. Magnum Club offers bonuses and offers based on customer interests, and its privacy policy describes purchase and application information [7]. Additional personalisation might encourage sales while making shoppers less comfortable about how much the company knows. Kazakhstan’s Personal Data Law establishes principles including lawfulness and confidentiality [8]. Before any new use, the privacy and legal teams should review its purpose, access permissions and customer choices. A published policy alone cannot establish that a proposed AI workflow meets these obligations.

Global trade adds another responsibility. Magnum’s supplier portal provides routes for resident and non-resident suppliers [9]. Currency changes, transport costs and uncertain deliveries could affect purchases, although this does not establish an import share or an actual disruption. Procurement should compare delivered cost and reliability while preserving product standards and fair treatment. Cheap sourcing loses value if goods arrive too late or spoil before sale.

The CSR discussion in Weekly Record 2 distinguishes viable operations, legal compliance, fair treatment and voluntary community support. Charitable giving cannot compensate for misleading recommendations or ignored complaints. For the search trial, the digital team should compare errors in Kazakh and Russian, and a service manager should own corrections and escalation. Staff should be able to challenge suggestions without pressure to approve them. Any food-waste claim needs a baseline and a consistent measure. Appendix Table 2 applies these obligations to the proposed search process. Expansion should depend on reliable service and acceptable costs, with unresolved privacy or safety concerns stopping the trial.

Magnum creates value by bringing products together where households and businesses can buy them. Its retail and wholesale activities serve different purchasing needs [1]. A household buys a basket for personal use; a business may need repeated supplies. In both cases, availability and convenience matter. Revenue comes from sales. After paying for goods, the remaining margin must cover wages, premises, logistics and other operating costs before there is profit. An increase in sales is therefore not sufficient evidence that a new service pays for itself.

Stock connects this model to risk. Goods waiting on shelves tie up money, while missing products can lose a sale. Perishable goods add the possibility of waste. Assisted forecasting could help managers decide what to order, but poor stock records would also make its recommendations unreliable. The comparison should include forecast errors, unavailable products, waste and staff time. These are proposed measures, not reported results for Magnum.

The company identifies its legal form as an LLP, or ТОО [7]. Under Kazakhstan’s partnership law, participants generally risk their contributions, subject to statutory exceptions; the partnership remains responsible for its obligations. The participants’ general meeting is its highest governing body [10]. This separates ownership from daily execution without removing management accountability. The sources used here do not establish Magnum’s beneficial owners or internal approval limits, so neither is assumed.

Weekly Record 3 treats a category manager’s trial as intrapreneurship within Magnum. A budget and stopping condition allow an idea to be tested without changing ownership. Magnum Club demonstrates digital customer interaction [7], but does not establish AI deployment. Combining the three records supports a narrower investment decision: improve ordering before expanding personalisation. If stock records prove unreliable during promotions, the verdict changes from pilot to delay until records are reconciled. Appendix Table 3 tests this changed assumption against costs and service outcomes.

Adapt product search. Carrefour introduced Hopla in France in June 2023 [11]. Its later announcement describes Hopla+ and shopping through ChatGPT [12]. Magnum could adapt the underlying catalogue search rather than copy the whole service. Questions in Kazakh and Russian should return products from the relevant catalogue with accurate availability. Ordinary search and staff assistance should remain available. The benefit depends on successful shopping, not on how fluent the reply sounds.

Pilot demand forecasting. Carrefour and SAS described using AI to support its supply chain [13]. This supports testing the process, not assuming the same return at Magnum. A trial should compare assisted forecasts with current ordering under comparable conditions. Category managers should approve orders and record corrections, including problems caused by promotions or missing stock data.

Adopt the principle of supplier accountability. Carrefour’s supplier ethics charter covers working conditions, safety and confidential reporting [14]. Magnum already has corporate rules [6], so the useful transfer is to check that purchasing decisions and complaint handling put those commitments into practice. It is not a reason to introduce another policy without checking the existing arrangements.

Delay additional personalisation based on shopping histories. Carrefour’s newer shopping service includes purchase-history suggestions [12], but Magnum should first establish a clear purpose, acceptable data handling and a benefit beyond its existing loyalty offers. Reject fully autonomous order approval at this stage. This is a boundary for the proposed Magnum trial, not a claim that Carrefour operates without people. Local performance, costs and accountability remain unresolved. These different verdicts reflect the risks of each activity rather than a general decision to accept or refuse AI.

First, the inventory team and category managers should select a manageable product category and pilot assisted forecasting. Keep current ordering as the comparison and retain manual approval. Success would mean fewer stockouts and less waste, with benefits exceeding software and staff costs [13].

Second, the digital team should test catalogue search with equivalent Kazakh and Russian shopping questions. Store staff should check matches and availability, comparing errors across languages. The service manager should record corrections and complaints; expand only if shoppers find suitable products more reliably than with ordinary search [11], [12].

Third, the privacy and legal teams should review proposed uses of Magnum Club data before adding personalisation. Document the purpose, access and customer choices. Successful completion means that unnecessary data are excluded and the proposed use has an approved legal basis [7], [8].

Finally, procurement and store managers should review supplier complaints and delivery exceptions together. Record resolution and recurrence. Success would mean fewer repeated issues and quicker resolution while product standards are maintained. This tests whether Magnum’s existing commitments influence purchasing and service [6].

chapters.title: Introduction
lines: Hello, my name is Kniazev Daniil, and I am from group AIB-2602.
And I would like to tell you about Magnum Cash&Carry’s human–AI operating model.

chapters.title: Opening position
lines: Magnum Cash&Carry should pilot AI demand forecasting while keeping people responsible for approving orders.
I will explain this proposal using Carrefour as a comparison.
People also handle exceptions.
Routine data checks can run automatically.
This fits a retailer serving household and wholesale customers.
My Week 3 stress test identified a condition:
stock records must match what is actually available before a forecasting trial begins.

chapters.title: Week 5 process map, bottleneck and KPI
lines: The process is replenishment, from checking sales and stock to approving an order and receiving goods.
Magnum publishes supplier and product acceptance rules, including remaining shelf life.
Its detailed workflow is not public, so the current map is a baseline to confirm with staff.
The suspected bottleneck is reconciling stock and promotion information before ordering.
My main KPI is shelf availability:
successful availability checks divided by all scheduled checks.
The proposed six-month target is 98 percent,
with waste and ordering costs monitored alongside it.

chapters.title: Week 4 human–AI task allocation matrix
lines: The matrix separates four categories.
Human Only covers final order approval.
The category manager checks quantities, shelf life and the budget because someone must remain accountable for the commitment.
This applies the textbook’s distinction between authority and responsibility.
Human + AI covers promotion planning.
Staff compare model suggestions with local events and supplier constraints, then decide what to change.
Participative leadership gives employees a way to challenge forecasts and contributes their store knowledge.
AI Executes with Human Review covers producing a demand forecast and draft quantities.
The manager checks these against recent sales, physical stock and known promotions before approval.
Automated covers fixed checks for missing fields and stale data, plus logging approved orders.
These routine rules require no model judgment.
The allocation follows the textbook’s planning and control cycle:
set standards, compare outcomes and correct deviations.

chapters.title: Human review, escalation and manual fallback
lines: If records disagree or the system fails,
staff stop the affected recommendation and alert the category manager.
Unresolved supply problems go to the supply-chain lead; technical faults go to IT.
The manual fallback uses a physical count and verified sales to prepare an order for the same manager’s approval.
NIST supports defined oversight, training and a non-AI alternative.

chapters.title: Carrefour comparison and transfer verdict
lines: Carrefour provides the comparison.
In January 2019, SAS reported that Carrefour selected its forecasting system after eighteen months of testing,
using store, warehouse and online data.
The announcement describes intended improvements, not a measured return for Magnum.
My verdict is PILOT.
Magnum needs its own data checks and comparison with existing ordering.
If stock accuracy fails, the verdict becomes DELAY.

chapters.title: First action and conditions for expansion
lines: First, select one store and category,
establish the baseline and practise manual ordering.
Expand only if availability reaches the proposed target,
forecast error improves and the net benefit remains positive after software and staff costs.

a3.claim: Magnum’s discounts create value that its weekly message fails to turn into purchases; AI can close that gap only behind a human check and a Kazakhstan data boundary, so Magnum should adapt Carrefour’s AI copywriting, adopt its data controls and delay its personalisation.

visuals.title: Company B: Magnum Cash&Carry and the value it promises
visuals.comment: Magnum sells savings and loyalty: a weekly discount catalogue, Magnum Club bonuses and offers such as a 30% Nivea bonus [28]. With 9.8% annual inflation [4], saving is the core household value. Club membership (2M+) is Magnum’s own figure [24], so the essay relies on customer-facing evidence.

visuals.title: The customer journey and where it breaks
visuals.comment: Value appears at every stage, but the weak link is between Consideration and Purchase. Shoppers can compare 51 deals [23] yet are not told where or how to buy, despite four store formats [28] and Magnum Go delivery [25]. This gap, not discount depth, is the essay’s problem.

visuals.title: The weekly Пайда page: strong attention, no next step
visuals.comment: The Пайда page confirms the gap. Its banner earns attention, but the promise of “up to 60%” was not met that week (maximum 53%), and the only instruction is to “keep following Пайда” [23]. For budget shoppers this weakens trust and leaves no next step.

visuals.title: What the 51 Пайда deals actually offer
visuals.comment: The data refine the insight: four of the six deepest discounts are non-food, while eggs, bananas and chicken fillet sit at 18–22% [23]. The biggest discount is not the most useful one for a family basket, so a tool ranking offers by discount alone would repeat this pattern.

visuals.title: Same task, two approaches: the method
visuals.comment: To test whether AI helps, both approaches used the same 51-product list and four criteria [23]. The baseline is Magnum’s published text, assumed human-written; the AI draft followed a prompt restricted to list facts. The method is transparent but small: one week, one message.

visuals.title: The result: same task, two outputs
visuals.comment: The AI draft met all four criteria, the baseline one. AI made the message specific and actionable, but customer response was not tested. The draft also named Magnum Go [25] without confirming Пайда prices apply there [23] and chose a non-food deal, echoing Visual 4. Human review remains essential.

visuals.title: Proposed workflow with a human gate
visuals.comment: The workflow places a human gate before anything reaches customers: AI drafts, a copywriter checks every price and claim, and the brand manager approves. Monitoring feeds the next brief; a manual template keeps campaigns running if the tool fails. This is a proposed pilot, not Magnum’s current system [7], [27].

visuals.title: From data to information, inside Kazakhstan’s rules
visuals.comment: The data boundary is a design choice, not paperwork. Only the public promo list reaches the AI tool; member data stays in Kazakhstan under the Personal Data Law’s consent and transfer rules [7]. The AI Law also requires telling users when services use AI [27].

visuals.title: Four risks, each with a control and an owner
visuals.comment: Privacy is the most serious risk: a leak of members’ data cannot be undone, and Kazakh law sets strict conditions [7], [24]. Its control keeps personal data out of prompts. An automatic price check plus sign-off controls reliability; a weekly food-staple rule controls bias. Residual risk: human error and unclear AI-labelling rules [27].

visuals.title: What Magnum should take from Carrefour, and on what terms
visuals.comment: Carrefour’s Hopla shows the opportunity and the cost [29]. Magnum should adapt AI content generation, used on 2,000+ Carrefour product sheets [12], adding fact checks and Kazakh review; adopt the data controls Carrefour introduced after a €2.25 million CNIL fine [26]; and delay purchase-history personalisation and ChatGPT shopping [19]. Next: a four-week pilot tracking orders and price complaints.
